title: Cancellation and timeouts
goal: By the end you can make CPU loops and blocking calls respond to cancellation, keep CancellationException flowing instead of swallowing it, run suspending cleanup after a cancel, and choose between withTimeout and withTimeoutOrNull.
opening:
Halfway through the afternoon, the phone rings. The guests can't come: dinner is off. The cook turns the oven down, puts a lid on the soup and takes the sauce off the heat. She hears the news between two steps of a recipe, when she glances at her phone.

Her helper in the corner is picking small stones out of a big sack of lentils. He never looks up between lentils, so he hears nothing, and he sorts the whole sack.

Coroutines are called off the same way. It's natural to think `cancel()` stops the code, but it only asks, and the code has to look up. Structured concurrency sent a cancel down the tree, and Dispatchers and the coroutine context ended with a question: what does a coroutine do when it's cancelled in the middle of a long loop, or inside a blocking call?

In this lesson, we'll watch a cancel reach a coroutine between steps and miss a busy loop, stop a `catch` from eating it, return a borrowed pan after it, and put a timer on the whole thing. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A coroutine on `Dispatchers.Default` runs `for (lentil in sack) if (isStone(lentil)) stones++` over two million lentils, with no suspend calls inside the loop. Another coroutine calls `job.cancel()` halfway through. What happens?
options: The loop stops at once, because `cancel()` stops the coroutine's thread
The loop stops at the next lentil, because the compiler adds a check to every loop
The loop runs to the end, and only then does the job finish as cancelled
`cancel()` throws `IllegalStateException`, because the coroutine is busy
warmup.why: Cancellation is cooperative. `cancel()` only marks the job as cancelling. The coroutine notices at its next suspension point or explicit check, and this loop has neither, so it sorts all two million lentils first, like the helper who never looks up. Java's `Future.cancel(true)` has the same limit: it sets a flag that somebody has to read.

sections.h: Never swallow the CancellationException that carries the cancel

aside.title: Is cancelling a coroutine the same as interrupting its thread?
aside.body: No, though the two ideas are cousins. A cancel marks the coroutine's job and leaves the thread alone, so `Thread.sleep` and other blocking JDK calls don't notice it. An interrupt marks a thread, and suspension points such as `delay` ignore it. The job's state also lasts: it reaches every child in the tree, and no `catch` can clear it, while catching `InterruptedException` clears the flag. The last section of this lesson shows `runInterruptible`, which turns a cancel into an interrupt for the blocking code that needs one.

sections.h: A timeout is a cancel with a timer, and blocking calls don't hear it
sections.body:
Before a big dinner, the cook also sets a kitchen timer on the bread order: if the bakery hasn't answered in a few minutes, she bakes her own. `withTimeout(d) { ... }` is that timer. It runs the block, and when `d` runs out, it cancels the block. The cancel is the ordinary kind from the first section: the block stops at its next suspension point, and `withTimeout` throws `TimeoutCancellationException`. `withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... }` does the same, but returns `null` instead of throwing:

```kotlin
val answer = withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { bakery.ask("sourdough") }
    ?: "no answer: bake our own"
```

```java
// Java equivalent: a fallback value when the future is late
String answer = bakery.askAsync("sourdough")
    .completeOnTimeout("no answer: bake our own", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .join();
```

Prefer `withTimeoutOrNull` when a timeout is an outcome you expect, as it is here. `TimeoutCancellationException` is a subclass of `CancellationException`, and that has a surprising effect. Inside `launch`, a timeout looks like an ordinary cancel, so a child that times out inside `coroutineScope` lets the scope finish normally, and nobody hears about it. If a timeout should fail the caller, turn it into a real error: `withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } ?: error("the bakery never answered")`.

A timer is still a cancel, and a cancel still only asks. So what happens when the block is stuck in a blocking call, one that holds its thread until it returns? The bakery from lesson 4 of this track still has an old order line, `BakeryHotline`, whose `ask` blocks the thread until somebody picks up. Let's wait 300 ms, and let the bakery take 1.5 s. `TimeoutsAndBlocking`, in the Try it below, tries four shapes, with `Thread.sleep` standing in for the call:

```text
withTimeout { delay }                              threw TimeoutCancellationException   after   307 ms
withTimeoutOrNull { delay }                        returned null                        after   304 ms
withTimeout { withContext(IO) { sleep } }          threw TimeoutCancellationException   after  1519 ms
withTimeoutOrNull { runInterruptible { sleep } }   returned null                        after   301 ms
```

The two `delay` lines stopped on time. The third line is the trap. The timer fired at 300 ms, but a thread blocked in `Thread.sleep` isn't at a suspension point. The thread stayed on the old phone line, listening to it ring, long after the timer had given up. Only when the call ended at 1.5 s did `withContext` notice the cancel and throw. The `Dispatchers.IO` thread, from the pool for blocking calls, was stuck the whole time. When the blocking call is the whole block, with no suspension at all, the timeout is ignored entirely, and the late answer comes back as if nothing had happened.

The fourth line is the fix. `runInterruptible(dispatcher) { ... }` runs blocking code on that dispatcher, and when the coroutine is cancelled, it interrupts the thread. It turns the resulting `InterruptedException` back into a `CancellationException`, so the caller sees an ordinary cancel:

```kotlin
withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) {
    runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { hotline.ask("sourdough") }   // interrupted on cancel
}
```

```java
// Java equivalent: give up after the timeout and interrupt the worker
Future<String> f = io.submit(() -> hotline.ask("sourdough"));
try { return f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }
catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); return null; }   // interrupts the blocked thread
```

Here the kitchen picture breaks. A cook can put the phone down whenever she likes. `runInterruptible` can only interrupt, and that helps only if the blocking call listens for interrupts. `Thread.sleep` and `BlockingQueue.take` do. A read from an old-style `java.net.Socket` network connection doesn't, and database drivers vary, so give such a client its own timeout as well.

**A timeout is a cancel with a timer. A blocking call hears it only through `runInterruptible`.**

That covers the places a cancel can get lost. A cancel, though, is the polite way for a coroutine to end. The next lesson takes the rude one: a coroutine that fails.

compare.title: Stopping a CPU loop: Future.cancel(true) vs Job.cancel()

java.title: LentilSort.java

kotlin.title: LentilSort.kt

compare.note: Both models are cooperative, and both loops need the same explicit check, once every thousand lentils. The difference is what carries the request. Java's interrupt is a flag on one thread. It doesn't reach other threads the task started, and catching `InterruptedException` clears it, so a careless `catch` loses it for good. A coroutine's cancel is a state on its job. It reaches every child in the tree, it stays set whatever you catch, and every suspension point in the library checks it for you, so most coroutine code needs no explicit check at all. Only CPU loops like this one, and blocking calls (which need `runInterruptible`), have to be taught to look up.

worked.title: Make an oven watcher stop cleanly

steps.say: The community kitchen has shared ovens. This function books one, then checks every 5 seconds whether the bread is done. When the cook calls the evening off, the function seems to hang, and the oven stays booked, so nobody else can use it. Find the three problems before you read on.
Problem 1: `catch (e: Exception)` swallows the `CancellationException` from `delay`, so a cancelled watcher spins. Catch only the oven's own error, and let the cancel through.

Problem 2: the release suspends in a cancelled coroutine, so it throws before the phone even rings. Wrap it in `NonCancellable`, with its own short timeout, so a phone nobody answers can't hold up the evening.
Problem 3: nothing bounds the whole wait. Give the caller a deadline, and treat running out as an expected outcome rather than an exception.

Self-check: the timeout in step 3 cancels `waitForBread` while it is suspended in `delay`. Trace what happens. (The `delay` throws `TimeoutCancellationException`, which passes the narrow `catch`. The `finally` releases the oven under `NonCancellable`, and `withTimeoutOrNull` turns the exception into `null`.)

lab.title: Fix four cancellation bugs in the kitchen

drill.title: A cancellable job from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `suspend fun labelJars(jars: List<Jar>, loan: Loan)` that runs on `Dispatchers.Default`, checks for cancellation every 500 jars, and calls `label(jar)`, which can throw `LabelException` (log it and skip that jar). It must always return the borrowed label printer with the suspending `loan.giveBack()`, even after a cancel.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: Cancellation is cooperative. `cancel()` marks the job, and the coroutine stops at its next suspension point or explicit check. CPU loops need `ensureActive()`, `isActive` or `yield()`.

Cancellation travels as `CancellationException`. `runCatching`, `catch (e: Exception)` and `catch (e: Throwable)` all catch it, so rethrow it or catch narrower types. Catching it never undoes the cancel.
In a cancelled coroutine every suspension point throws at once. Run suspending cleanup in `finally` inside `withContext(NonCancellable)`, and never pass `NonCancellable` to `launch` or `async`.

`withTimeout` throws `TimeoutCancellationException` (a `CancellationException`), and `withTimeoutOrNull` returns `null`. Inside `launch`, a timeout doesn't fail the parent unless you turn it into an error.
The limit: a cancel only asks. Blocking code hears it only through `runInterruptible`, and only if the call responds to interrupts; for the rest, give the client its own timeout.
closing:
We started with a dinner called off halfway, a cook who heard the news between steps, and a helper who sorted the whole sack. Coroutines hear a cancel only at suspension points and checks, carry it as `CancellationException`, and need `NonCancellable` to clean up after it. A timeout is the same cancel with a timer.

Now search your own code for `runCatching` and `catch (e: Exception)` around suspend calls. Each one that doesn't rethrow `CancellationException` turns the next cancel into a list of fake failures.

Next, we'll burn a dish instead of calling it off. When a coroutine fails, who hears about it, and how do you stop one burnt tray from spoiling the rest?

quiz.q: `val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) { while (true) { weigh(nextJar()) } }`, where `weigh` and `nextJar` are plain functions. You call `job.cancelAndJoin()`. What happens?
options: It returns at once, because `cancel` stops the coroutine
It returns after the current loop iteration
It never returns: the loop has no suspension point and never checks
The caller gets a `CancellationException` thrown from `cancelAndJoin`
quiz.why: Nothing in the loop looks at the job, so the cancel is never noticed, and `cancelAndJoin` waits forever. Add `ensureActive()` or `yield()` to the loop, or loop on `while (isActive)`. The tempting "after the current iteration" would need a check at the top of each iteration, and there is none.

quiz.q: A coroutine was cancelled while it waited in `delay`. Its `finally` block must call the suspending `desk.giveBack(ticket)`. Which line does that correctly?
options: `try { desk.giveBack(ticket) } catch (e: CancellationException) { }`
`withContext(NonCancellable) { desk.giveBack(ticket) }`
`launch(NonCancellable) { desk.giveBack(ticket) }`
`GlobalScope.launch { desk.giveBack(ticket) }`
quiz.why: Inside `withContext(NonCancellable)` suspension points don't throw, so `giveBack` runs to the end, and the cancel carries on afterwards. Catching the exception just loses the call. `launch(NonCancellable)` and `GlobalScope` both start a coroutine outside the tree that nothing waits for, so the program can finish before the pan goes back.

options: `done`, after about 100 ms
Nothing: `coroutineScope` throws `TimeoutCancellationException`
`done`, after about 1,000 ms
Nothing: the program hangs
quiz.why: `TimeoutCancellationException` is a `CancellationException`, so the child counts as cancelled, not failed, and the scope completes normally. If a timeout must fail the caller, write `withTimeoutOrNull(100) { ... } ?: error("timed out")`.

quiz.q: `withTimeout(500) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(3_000) } }`. How long does the caller wait, and what does it get?
options: About 500 ms, then `TimeoutCancellationException`
About 500 ms, then `null`
About 3 s, then `TimeoutCancellationException`
About 3 s, then the block's result
quiz.why: The timer fires at 500 ms and cancels the coroutine, but `Thread.sleep` doesn't see it. When the sleep ends, `withContext` checks, finds the job cancelled, and the timeout comes out as the exception. `runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO)` would interrupt the sleep at 500 ms.

quiz.q: From the executors track: a task is blocked in `Thread.sleep(5_000)` when someone calls `future.cancel(true)` on it. What happens to the task?
options: Nothing until the sleep ends, then it carries on
The thread is stopped and the task's `finally` blocks are skipped
The future completes normally with `null`
`sleep` throws `InterruptedException` at once, and the task can clean up and stop
quiz.why: `cancel(true)` interrupts the worker thread, and `sleep` responds to interrupts by throwing. What the task does next is up to its code: restore the flag and stop, or swallow it and carry on. That is the Java version of `runInterruptible`.

flashcards.front: Does `job.cancel()` stop a CPU loop with no suspend calls?
flashcards.back: No. Cancellation is cooperative: the loop must call `ensureActive()` or `yield()`, or check `isActive`.

flashcards.front: What does a suspension point such as `delay` do in a cancelled coroutine?
flashcards.back: It throws `CancellationException` at once, without suspending.

flashcards.front: Why is `runCatching { suspendCall() }` risky inside a coroutine?
flashcards.back: It catches every `Throwable`, `CancellationException` included, so the loop carries on in a coroutine that is still cancelled. Rethrow `CancellationException`.

flashcards.front: How do you call a suspending cleanup function in `finally` after a cancel?
On timeout, what do `withTimeout` and `withTimeoutOrNull` do?

flashcards.back: No. Blocking calls ignore cancellation. Wrap them in `runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { ... }` so the thread is interrupted.

flashcards.front: How does a plain suspend function, with no scope, check for cancellation?

terms.plain: The handle to a coroutine's life: you can wait for it or cancel it.
Cancelling only asks; the code stops when it next checks or reaches a suspension point.
A call to a suspend function such as `delay`, `await` or `withContext`. Library ones check for cancellation.
The exception that carries a cancel through the coroutine's code. Catching it without rethrowing breaks cancellation.
A job that is always active. `withContext(NonCancellable)` lets cleanup suspend after a cancel.
What `withTimeout` throws. It is a `CancellationException`, so a parent treats it as a cancel, not a failure.
Runs blocking code on a dispatcher and interrupts its thread if the coroutine is cancelled.

explain_back.prompt: A friend wrapped every call in the evening's supplier round in `runCatching`, "so one busy line never stops the round". When the dinner was called off, the log listed seventeen failed calls that had never failed. Explain what happened and how you'd change the code.
explain_back.answer: Calling the dinner off cancelled the coroutine running the round. A cancel reaches the code as a CancellationException thrown from the next suspension point, and runCatching catches every Throwable, so it caught that too and logged the call in progress as failed. Catching it didn't undo the cancel: the coroutine was still cancelled, so the next call threw at its first suspension point, got caught and logged the same way, and so on through all seventeen remaining calls. Then the function returned normally. I'd keep the per-call error handling, but rethrow CancellationException before logging anything, or catch only the exceptions a phone call is expected to throw. Then a cancel ends the round at the call in progress, and any cleanup that suspends goes in a finally inside withContext(NonCancellable).

deeper.body:
A `CancellationException` doesn't always mean "I was cancelled". If you `await()` a `Deferred` that someone else cancelled, `await` throws `CancellationException` in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 KDoc calls this a legacy behavior that can't be changed compatibly: your coroutine then ends as "cancelled", so its parent isn't told and the work quietly stops. If you catch it, call `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` in the `catch`. It throws only if *your* coroutine was cancelled, so after it you know the exception came from the thing you awaited, and you can turn it into a real error.

The library also gives a **prompt cancellation guarantee**. If a coroutine is cancelled while suspended, it resumes with `CancellationException` even when the value it was waiting for had already arrived. `withContext` checks for cancellation both on entry and when its block returns. So `val pan = withContext(io) { desk.lendBlocking() }` can lose a pan: the block borrowed it, the caller was cancelled in the meantime, and the result is thrown away. Borrow and give back inside the same block, or use the cleanup function of `CancellableContinuation.resume` when you write the bridge yourself (lesson 1 of this track).

Timeouts have one more subtle rule. The KDoc says cancellation on timeout "may happen at any time, even after the block finishes executing but before the caller gets resumed". So never write `withTimeout { pan = desk.lend() }` and expect `pan` to be either unset or yours. Borrow outside the timeout, or give it back in the block's own `finally`.

Flows, which lesson 7 of this track introduces, have the same cooperative rule at a smaller scale. A `flow { }` builder checks for cancellation at every `emit`, but `list.asFlow()` and `(1..n).asFlow()` don't, so add `.cancellable()` to a long one that must stop on time.

Finally, `runBlocking` bridges in the other direction. If the thread blocked in `runBlocking` is interrupted, the coroutine is cancelled, and `runBlocking` throws `InterruptedException`. That's how coroutine code called from a plain Java worker thread can still be stopped by an executor's `shutdownNow()`.
